transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-26 15:00 UTC
Duration: 56 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Lila (CTO), Arjun (Head Infra), Priya (SecEng), Mateo (ML Platform)
---
Summary (auto): quick intro, high-level requirements for an air-gapped/private deployment, primary constraints: hardware availability, offline update procedure, key compliance asks (audit logs, KMS, SSO), discuss tradeoffs hosted vs dedicated vs private and fallback modes, agree next steps to ship security pack and propose a hardware footprint.
---
[00:00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we got a few voice notes from arjun on the invite about hardware windows so we'll try to keep this tightly scoped
[00:00:10] Lila: thanks maya, yeah we're looking to evaluate options for a fully segregated inference stack for genomics pipelines, uh regulatory environment, very tight data residency, no external egress basically
[00:00:25] Ethan: cool, the way we usually approach this is map requirements -> propose footprint + update cadence -> run a short pilot in your lab, then iterate. can you outline the must-haves?
[00:00:35] Arjun: sure, must-haves: no outbound internet from the inference nodes, updates only through physically transported media, must have signed packages, HSM or KMIP-backed key storage, and audit logs that we can retain for 7 years. also limited rack power per site, so we can't assume full-on H100 farms.
[00:00:55] Priya: and from security: SSO integration is required for operator access, SAML ok, we also need RBAC and ability to rotate keys without internet. we need detailed logs per request including model version and token counts for compliance.
[00:01:12] Maya: got it. so offline updates, zero egress, long-term audit retention, RBAC + SSO, and constrained power. anything on throughput or latency SLOs?
[00:01:25] Mateo: throughput is moderate: peak 80 concurrent requests, mostly short sequences 128-512 tokens. latency SLOs are 400-800 ms p95 for single-turn inference in product pathways, but batch async workloads can be higher. we also have large batch recompute jobs for retraining support but those run in air-gapped batch windows.
[00:01:47] Ethan: okay that helps. On the hardware side, arjun mentioned limited racks — do you have specific GPU models you're buying or prefer?
[00:01:56] Arjun: procurement is slow right now. we have some spare A100 40GB nodes but replacement cycle is long. H100 would be ideal but budget and power are issues. Some sites might accept smaller T4 or L4 class for low-priority workloads.
[00:02:12] Lila: important point: for production inference that impacts clinicians we need predictable latency, so we'd likely carve a small pool of higher-memory GPUs and offload non-critical to lower-power nodes.
[00:02:23] Maya: sounds reasonable. quick clarification — when you say signed packages for updates, do you mean you want a media-based installer that we ship and you apply, or do you want a mechanism where we push signed artifacts to an internal repo that your team pulls?
[00:02:36] Priya: media-based. internal policy forbids external pulls. updates must come in via encrypted USB crates with chain-of-custody and signed manifests.
[00:02:48] Ethan: yeah we've implemented this model with two customers — we generate a signed tar.gz with version metadata, signed with Redwood's code-signing key and verified by a local agent that runs in the customer enclave. agent does offline verification against a customer-managed HSM. can be adapted to KMIP.
[00:03:05] Arjun: the verification step is critical — we need to be able to cryptographically verify the image and the model weights. we also want the ability to rollback quickly in the event of a regression.
[00:03:16] Maya: rollback support is built-in in our private runtime — you can pin model versions and we ship a small control plane that can be run in your VPC or on-prem. in air-gapped mode the control plane operates from within your network and accepts only signed packages.
[00:03:28] Lila: what's the footprint for the control plane? we have to fit within a small management cluster.
[00:03:34] Ethan: control plane is lightweight: usually 2-3 VMs for small deployments — API/control + operator + metrics. for larger clusters we recommend HA with 3 masters, but for your use case we can scale down. it doesn't require GPUs.
[00:03:46] Mateo: what about KV cache and persistent state? our pipelines leverage long-lived kv caches for long sequence workloads, we want to avoid warm-up penalties.
[00:03:56] Ethan: we can configure local NVMe-backed KV caches per GPU host. cache can be snapshotted and included in the offline artifact if you want checkpointed state to be transplanted during updates — though that makes the media size larger.
[00:04:11] Priya: how big are those snapshots? network's off so we have to physically transport them. some of our caches are several hundred GBs per node. that's potentially painful.
[00:04:21] Ethan: understood; one approach is hierarchical caching — keep a small hot prefix in NVMe and let the cold KV build during low-traffic windows. We'll share recommended cache sizing for your token distributions.
[00:04:33] Arjun: can the runtime run quantized models? smaller memory footprint helps a lot.
[00:04:38] Maya: yes we support int8/4 quantization profiles — tradeoffs are slight accuracy delta versus 2-4x memory reduction. we can produce quantization evaluation against a small eval set you provide.
[00:04:49] Lila: security question — can we bring our own key material and manage rotation with our HSM?
[00:04:54] Ethan: yes, BYOK via KMIP or local HSM. For true air-gapped environments we support HSM provisioning on-site and local key wrapping. rotation is handled locally; Redwood control plane will call local KMIP endpoints only.
[00:05:06] Priya: any third-party telemetry? we can't have telemetry leaving the enclave.
[00:05:10] Maya: no telemetry leaves without explicit agreement. in private mode telemetry is optional and can be stored in your network — we typically ship logs to your ELK/Splunk inside the VPC.
[00:05:20] Mateo: backup windows — how do we handle rolling restarts and patch windows? our clinic hours are tight (02:00-04:00 local), can't have major downtime outside that slot.
[00:05:31] Ethan: we support canary rollouts with automatic fallback. for air-gapped installs the update is staged: operator places signed media on a staging node, operator triggers a canary rollout to a single rack, we run health checks, if green we'll roll incrementally. rollback is metadata-only and quick if an issue is found.
[00:05:45] Arjun: do you have any automation for signing artifacts that integrates with our CI so we can produce customer-signed packages ourselves?
[00:05:52] Ethan: yes, we can provide a signing tool and verification agent. customer can sign artifacts using their key or accept our signed builds. we prefer customer signing in high-reg environments.
[00:06:01] Lila: let's talk latency again — you're talking about canary and rollouts — but for clinician-facing endpoints we need p95 under 800 ms consistently. with A100 40GB or H100 you'd meet that — have you measured p95 on quantized vs full fp16 models?
[00:06:15] Ethan: measurements vary by model. for a 7B-class model quantized to int8 on A100 we typically see p95 around 250-350 ms for 128 token sequences. for larger models it increases; we can provide benchmark artifacts. also need to account for soft real-time constraints with batch size and concurrency.
[00:06:31] Maya: we'll attach benchmark spreadsheets from similar customers.
[00:06:35] Priya: audit logs — what fields do you capture? we need model id, version, request id, timestamp, user id, token counts, decision path.
[00:06:44] Ethan: we capture request id, model id/version, tokens in/out, latency, node id, and any classifier labels (if configured). Logs can be exported in JSONL to your internal SIEM. They remain inside the VPC by default.
[00:06:55] Lila: and retention?
[00:06:57] Maya: configurable. default is 90 days, but we can set to 7 years per your compliance as long as you have storage.
[00:07:05] Arjun: on physical constraints — some of our labs only have 10A circuits per rack. what are realistic GPU density options for low power?
[00:07:15] Ethan: with 10A per rack you're limited. We recommend lower-power accelerators (L4 or T4) for non-critical workloads; for critical endpoints you might need to provision fewer higher-power GPUs in separate racks. We'll provide a pro forma power vs throughput chart.
[00:07:30] Mateo: what about model updates frequency? our clinical models will be updated quarterly, but safety patches could be monthly. what's the minimal operational overhead for that cadence?
[00:07:40] Maya: operationally quarterly model updates via signed media is straightforward. monthly security patches are doable — we recommend bundling minor patches into a monthly maintenance bundle to reduce operator churn.
[00:07:51] Arjun: any recommended approach for automated verification of model behavior post-deploy? we want to run a local eval suite as part of the canary.
[00:07:58] Ethan: yes, we can package an eval harness that runs a smoke test and a set of regression prompts during the canary. it reports back a binary pass/fail and metrics that show distribution shifts. all results stay local.
[00:08:10] Priya: how do you handle model provenance — we need full chain-of-custody for model weights.
[00:08:15] Maya: we include provenance metadata: source hash, training commit id if available, signer, and a manifest with checksums for all artifacts. for models onboarded by Redwood we can include the origin and vetting notes.
[00:08:26] Lila: what's your recommended first pilot scope? we'd like to validate offline update process and latency on the A100 nodes we have.
[00:08:33] Maya: pilot recommendation: 2 racks (or 4 GPU hosts) in your lab, one staging control plane VM, signed update flow test, a canary rollout with our eval harness, and end-to-end audit log export to your SIEM. duration 3-4 weeks.
[00:08:47] Mateo: perf testing — can you simulate our 80-concurrency peak? we don't want surprises when we scale.
[00:08:53] Ethan: yes we'll run synthetic load with realistic token distributions. if cache warmup matters we can pre-seed caches. there might be scheduling variability at high concurrency; we'll tune batching parameters and KV cache sizes.
[00:09:05] Arjun: okay let's dive into packaging — how big is the typical offline artifact for a single model + runtime?
[00:09:11] Ethan: depends on model size and cache. a 7B model quantized might be 2-8 GB; a 70B model could be 30-150 GB depending on quantization. runtime + control plane bits are small (hundreds of MB). if you include cache snapshots you could be hundreds of GBs.
[00:09:28] Priya: that's a problem for logistics. do you support streamed diff updates instead of full-image distribution?
[00:09:34] Maya: for air-gapped we can support delta updates if you have a baseline image. the signing and verification process works on diffs as well, which cuts media size.
[00:09:42] Lila: competitor question: we looked at some vendors that promised full offline installs but required AMIs or cloud linkage. how is Redwood different?
[00:09:50] Maya: Redwood provides a standalone control plane that runs entirely in your network. many cloud-managed vendors maintain cloud dependencies. we can run with zero external dependency if you prefer, and we have prior customers who are fully hermetic.
[00:10:01] Arjun: any limitations if we go fully hermetic? e.g., no remote support or remote health-checks?
[00:10:07] Ethan: remote support is limited; we offer a support playbook and can run pre-signed diagnostic bundles you execute locally and send the signed results via secure channels. there's also an option to set up a one-way data diode to a jump server if policy allows.
[00:10:20] Mateo: about fallback: if a node fails and we need to route to hosted Redwood temporarily, is that possible? our policy currently forbids egress to external clouds for PHI.
[00:10:30] Maya: we support a fallback policy but it requires contractual approval and additional safeguards. many customers don't enable automatic fallback in hermetic deployments; it's usually a planned DR procedure.
[00:10:42] Priya: what about SAML integration — can you integrate into our IdP with just internal endpoints?
[00:10:48] Ethan: yes, control plane calls your IdP endpoints inside the VPC. we can also support client cert auth for operator nodes.
[00:10:55] Lila: would you provide an SOW template for onsite installation and security review?
[00:11:00] Maya: yes, we'll include a draft SOW with the security checklist and hardware footprint.
[00:11:04] Arjun: pricing — approximate premium for private hermetic deployment vs hosted?
[00:11:10] Maya: private hermetic includes a platform fee plus deployment services. typically 2-4x hosted per-seat equivalent because of operational overhead, but dedicated commit options smooth unit economics. we'll send a high-level estimate.
[00:11:21] Lila: any training required for our operators?
[00:11:24] Ethan: ops training is part of the deployment; a 2-day onsite workshop covers update flows, rollback, and monitoring.
[00:11:31] Mateo: show me an example of the signed manifest format and the verification logs you capture.
[00:11:36] Maya: we'll attach a sample manifest and example verification logs in the security pack.
[00:11:40] Arjun: for the pilot, what are the minimal acceptance criteria?
[00:11:44] Maya: acceptance: successful offline update and rollback, p95 latency within agreed SLO for your test prompts, audit logs shipped to SIEM locally, signed verification workflow validated, and a handover training completed.
[00:11:57] Lila: sounds good. any blockers on Redwood side?
[00:12:00] Ethan: nothing immediate, but we'll need your network diagrams and maintenance windows to finalize the plan.
[00:12:06] Maya: ok let's capture next steps.
[00:12:09] Maya: action recap: we'll send security pack and SOW draft; ethan will propose footprint; arjun to send current rack power specs and maintenance windows; lila to confirm stakeholder list for pilot.
[00:12:22] Arjun: i'll send rack PDU specs and the procurement timeline.
[00:12:26] Priya: i'll pull together compliance controls and any SOC2 artifacts we need to map.
[00:12:30] Maya: great, we'll target the onsite workshop week of march 9th pending travel and your approval.
[00:12:37] Lila: ok thanks everyone.
[00:12:40] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up with materials later today.
